Endangered Species Act 
The ESA specifically prohibits the “take” of a listed endangered wildlife species on all lands (public or 
private). However, some listed threatened wildlife species have “take” protections if a 4(d) rule was 
established with the listing. The ESA does not provide the same take protections of plant species, except 
on federal land. Take is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or 
collect, or to engage in any such conduct.” 
Federal species protected under the ESA and evaluated in this biological report were based on the 
project-specific1 Information for Planning and Consultation (IPaC) list of endangered, threatened, 
non-essential experimental population (EXPN), and candidate species obtained through the USFWS’s 
online IPaC system database for Navajo County, Arizona (Appendix A) (USFWS 2024a). The IPaC also 
indicated that designated critical habitat is not present in the project area. In addition, review of the 
USFWS Critical Habitat Mapper indicates that critical habitat is not present in the project area (USFWS 
2024b). 
Species Evaluation 
The species analysis (i.e., occurrence and effects) in this biological report is based on the ESA standard of 
reasonably certain to occur (50 CFR 402.02). The potential for occurrence of each species was 
summarized according to the categories listed below. Because not all species are accommodated precisely 
by a given category (i.e., category definitions may be too restrictive), an expanded rationale for each 
category assignment is provided. Potential for occurrence categories are as follows. 
• Known to occur—the species has been documented in the project area by a reliable observer. 
• May occur—the project area is within the species’ currently known range, and vegetation 
communities, soils, etc., resemble those known to be used by the species. 
• Unlikely to occur—the project area is within the species’ currently known range, but vegetation 
communities, soils, etc., do not resemble those known to be used by the species, or the project 
area is clearly outside the species’ currently known range. 
Species listed by the USFWS were assigned to one of three categories of possible effect, in accordance 
with the following USFWS recommendations: 
• May affect, is likely to adversely affect—the proposed project is likely to adversely affect a listed 
species if 1) the species occurs or may occur in the project area and 2) any adverse effect on listed 
species may occur as a direct or indirect result of the proposed action or its interrelated or 
interdependent actions, and the effect is not discountable, insignificant, or beneficial.2 In the 
event that the overall effect of the proposed action is beneficial to the listed species but also 
is likely to cause some adverse effects, the proposed action “is likely to adversely affect” the 
listed species. 
 
1 An unofficial IPaC species list was requested since the project currently does not have a federal nexus that would trigger the 
need for an official IPaC species list. 
2 Beneficial effects are contemporaneous positive effects without any adverse effects on the species. Insignificant effects relate to 
the size of the impact and should never reach the scale where take occurs. Discountable effects are those extremely unlikely to 
occur. Based on best judgment, a person would not 1) be able to meaningfully measure, detect, or evaluate insignificant effects, 
or 2) expect discountable effects to occur.

<!-- page 718 -->
Biological Resources Memorandum for the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project in Navajo County, Arizona / 
SWCA Project No. 83604 
18 
• May affect, is not likely to adversely affect—the project is not likely to adversely affect a listed 
species if 1) the species may occur but its presence has not been documented and/or surveys 
following approved protocol have been conducted with negative results, and/or 2) project activity 
effects on a listed species are expected to be discountable, insignificant, or completely beneficial. 
• No effect—the project will have no effect (including effects that may be beneficial, insignificant, 
or discountable) on a listed species if 1) the species is considered unlikely to occur (range, 
vegetation, soils, etc., are inappropriate), or 2) neither the species nor its sign were observed 
during surveys of the project area. 
• May affect, not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of—the project may affect individuals 
of an experimental population within the experimental population area. 
Because species not listed as threatened or endangered are not protected under the authority of the ESA, 
impact determinations for these species do not follow the above USFWS recommendations. Instead, the 
impact determinations for any species listed as candidate or proposed endangered/threatened and not 
protected under the ESA are as follows: 
• No impact—the project would have no impact on a species if 1) the species is considered 
unlikely to occur (range, vegetation, etc., are inappropriate) and 2) neither the species nor its sign 
was observed during surveys of the project area. 
• Beneficial impact—the project is likely to benefit the species, whether it is currently present 
or not, by creating or enhancing habitat elements known to be used by the species. 
• May impact individuals but is not likely to result in a trend toward federal listing or loss of 
viability—the project is not likely to adversely impact a species if 1) the species may occur but its 
presence has not been documented and 2) project activities would not result in disturbance 
to areas or habitat elements known to be used by the species. 
• May impact individuals and is likely to result in a trend toward federal listing or loss of 
viability—the project is likely to adversely impact a species if 1) the species is known to occur 
in the project area and 2) project activities would disturb areas or habitat elements known 
to be used by the species or would directly affect an individual.

* USFWS Status Definitions 
C = Candidate. Candidate species are those for which the USFWS has sufficient information on bi ological vulnerability and threats to support 
proposals to list as endangered or threatened under the ESA. However, proposed rules have not yet been issued because such ac tions are 
precluded at present by other listing activity. 
E = Endangered. An animal or plant species in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range.  
EXPN = Experimental Population, Non-essential. Experimental populations of a species designated under Section 10(j) of the ESA for which the 
USFWS, through the best available information, believes is not essential for the continued existence of the species. Regulatory restrictions are 
considerably reduced under an EXPN designation. 
T = Threatened. An animal or plant species which is likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion 
of its range. 
Migratory Bird Treaty Act 
The MBTA provides federal protection to nearly all birds native to North America, including their nests 
and eggs, on all lands (public or private). The MBTA does not protect nonnative bird species, and it does 
not protect certain native birds (quails, grouse, or turkeys, or their relatives). The MBTA defines “take” 
as “to pursue, hunt, take, capture, kill, attempt to take, capture, or kill, possess, offer for sale, sell, offer 
to barter, barter, offer to purchase, purchase, deliver for shipment, ship, export, import, cause to be 
shipped, exported, or imported, deliver for transportation, transport or cause to be transported, carry or 
cause to be carried, or receive for shipment, transportation, carriage, or export, any migratory bird, any 
part, nest, or egg of any such bird, or any product, whether or not manufactured, which consists, or is 
composed in whole or part, of any such bird or any part, nest, or egg thereof.” Take is prohibited without 
a permit. If birds, nests, or eggs are present in the project area and cannot be avoided, they must be 
relocated before construction begins, which would require an MBTA permit from the USFWS.

<!-- page 721 -->
Biological Resources Memorandum for the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project in Navajo County, Arizona / 
SWCA Project No. 83604 
21 
If non–western burrowing owl (Athene cunicularia hypugaea) MBTA-protected individuals or nests 
occur in the project area and cannot be avoided during construction, the nests and individuals will need to 
be relocated. The USFWS’s Destruction and Relocation of Migratory Bird Nest Contents Memorandum 
states that if a nest is completely inactive at the time of destruction or movement, a permit is not required 
to comply with the MBTA (USFWS 2018). If vegetation clearing is expected to take place during the 
nesting season (i.e., generally February through late August for songbirds, depending on the species and 
habitat; for raptors, it is generally January through late June [AZGFD 2022; Corman and Wise-Gervais 
2005]). It is recommended that a nesting bird survey be conducted before vegetation-clearing activities 
are performed to locate any active nests. In north-central Arizona, some bird species are multi-clutch 
species, which means that they nest multiple times during the nesting season. Measures should then be 
taken to protect the nest from destruction and to avoid a violation of the MBTA. To relocate or alter any 
non–burrowing owl MBTA-protected individuals or nests that are active, Stellar will need a permit from 
the USFWS for relocation. 
All the bird species listed in Table 2 are protected under the MBTA. 
The western burrowing owl is a common species throughout western North America. No individuals 
or indicators of burrow use (e.g., fresh whitewash, fresh pellets, feathers, or nest ornamentation) by the 
western burrowing owl were observed in the project area. However, suitable burrows without evidence 
of use were observed. Although no occurrence records for the species are known within 5 miles of the 
project area, the project area is within the predicted range by AZGFD; thus, the species could occupy the 
site (AZGFD 2024b). The Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners should be 
followed to avoid disturbance to the MBTA-protected burrowing owl (AZGFD 2009a) (Appendix B). 
Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act 
Bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) and golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) are protected under both the 
MBTA and the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (BGEPA) on all lands (public or private). 
The BGEPA prohibits anyone without a permit from “taking” eagles, their parts, eggs, or nests. Take is 
defined by the BGEPA as “to pursue, shoot, shoot at, poison, wound, kill, capture, trap, collect, molest, 
or disturb;” the BGEPA’s definition of “take” differs from the definition in the ESA in that it does not 
include habitat destruction or alteration, unless such damage “disturbs” an eagle. Disturb is defined as 
“to agitate or bother to a degree that causes, or is likely to cause, based on the best scientific information 
available, (1) injury to an eagle, (2) a decrease in its productivity, by substantially interfering with normal 
breeding, feeding, or sheltering behavior, or (3) nest abandonment, by substantially interfering with 
normal breeding, feeding, or sheltering behavior.” 
Bald eagles are found typically in association with water and nest and breed from December to June 
throughout the state of Arizona; however, they also winter throughout the state (Southwestern Bald Eagle 
Management Committee 2024). Golden eagles nest primarily on rock ledges or cliffs and occasionally 
in large trees at elevations ranging from 4,000 to 10,000 feet above mean sea level (AZGFD 2024a). 
Golden eagles are typically found in mountainous regions of open country, prairies, Arctic and alpine 
tundra, open wooded areas, and barren areas (AZGFD 2024a). Both bald and golden eagles are 
carnivores. Bald eagles primarily eat fish, but they will also eat birds, amphibians, reptiles, small 
mammals, carrion (dead animals), and carcasses of large mammals (cows, elk, deer, etc.) (Southwestern 
Bald Eagle Management Committee 2024). Golden eagles feed mainly on small mammals, as well as 
invertebrates, carrion, and other wildlife (AZGFD 2024a). 
The Probability of Presence Summary found in the IPaC report indicates that there is a high likelihood 
that bald eagles may be present in the project area except for just after the breeding season, when they 
likely disperse until the start of the next breeding season. Golden eagles are seldomly present in the

<!-- page 722 -->
Biological Resources Memorandum for the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project in Navajo County, Arizona / 
SWCA Project No. 83604 
22 
project area, with reports only in June, September, and October. These reports are likely dispersing 
individuals pre- and post-breeding (USFWS 2024a). In addition, the AZGFD Online Environmental 
Review Tool (ERT) results reported a record of occurrence for bald and golden eagles within 5 miles 
of the project area (AZGFD 2024b). With ranching being a big part of the economy in the area, other than 
dispersal, one thing that may attract both bald and golden eagles to the project is the potential for dead 
cattle. Eagles are unlikely to nest or breed in the project area. Until more information is known about the 
project design and activities, the overall effects to eagles are unknown, but unlikely to rise to the level of 
take as defined under the BGEPA. 
State of Arizona and Local Conservation Priorities 
The State of Arizona does not have an equivalent counterpart to the federal ESA, and there is no 
comparable permitting process for harm to wildlife during development. The AZGFD can provide an 
advisory role during the planning and permitting of energy infrastructure projects and may provide formal 
comments during state and local permitting processes. The AZGFD will also respond to requests for 
informal guidance from developers. The ERT may identify several categories of state conservation 
priorities, beyond the federal laws already addressed, as well as certain local conservation priorities 
identified at the county level. SWCA has included the results from the ERT query in this biological report 
in the event that stakeholders request consideration of these resources during the project’s planning and 
permitting process (Appendix C) (AZGFD 2024b). 
This section addresses the following resources: 
• SGCN 
• SERI 
• Special areas 
o Wildlife corridors and linkages 
o Important Bird Areas 
o Migratory Flyways 
o Ungulate Migration Routes 
o Important Connectivity Zones 
SGCN is a non-regulatory AZGFD status that lists wildlife of conservation priority in the state of Arizona 
(described nationally as Wildlife of Greatest Conservation Need). SGCN are species of vertebrates, 
crustaceans, and mollusks that rank high in the AZGFD vulnerability assessment and have been identified 
as priorities for immediate conservation action, as detailed in The Arizona Wildlife Conservation Strategy 
(2022–2032) (AZGFD 2022). Each species is assessed by the AZGFD in terms of vulnerability and 
assigned a Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3 ranking, with Tier 1 representing the highest threat level (AZGFD 
2022). 
The SGCN list may overlap species already discussed above under relevant federal laws. SGCN not 
otherwise protected by federal laws are not given additional protection under state law and are therefore 
not addressed in detail in this report. Appendix C provides the results of the ERT query, which identified 
17 SGCN species with occurrence records within 5 miles of the project area (see page 9 in Appendix C). 
Of those, black-throated sparrow (Amphispiza bilineata) and horned lark (Eremophila alpestris) were 
observed during the field reconnaissance of the project area. ESA species with records within 5 miles are 
discussed in Table 4. Some of the remaining species also may occur in the project area.

<!-- page 723 -->
Biological Resources Memorandum for the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project in Navajo County, Arizona / 
SWCA Project No. 83604 
23 
Finally, the ERT report indicates that four SERI, which are particular game species, are predicted to occur 
in or within a 5-mile radius of the project area, including America pronghorn (Antilocapra americana 
americana), mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), mountain lion (Puma concolor), and mourning dove 
(Zenaida macroura) (AZGFD 2024b) (see Appendix B). As Table 3 indicates, American pronghorn, mule 
deer, and mourning dove individuals or sign were observed during the field reconnaissance of the project 
area. SERI are not given special protection under state laws. 
The AZGFD is responsible for the management of SGCN and most SERI, although some SERI are also 
subject to MBTA rules regarding hunting. The AZGFD works with federal agencies and other partners 
toidentify wildlife movement areas and provides recommendations to preserve the function of those areas 
for wildlife movement. The AZGFD will also review the project as the state wildlife agency and the 
AZGFD may request additional survey or conservation (mitigation) for potential impacts to some of these 
species or their habitat. The AZGFD’s mitigation recommendations typically prioritize minimizing 
impacts to SGCN and SERI. The ERT also includes AZGFD recommendations for the project design and 
development to conserve vegetation and wildlife. The AZGFD has also published the following 
guidelines to minimize the impacts of development to wildlife: 
• Guidelines for Solar Development in Arizona (AZGFD 2010) 
• Wildlife Friendly Guidelines: Community and Project Planning (AZGFD 2009b) 
• Wildlife Compatible Fencing (AZGFD 2007) 
The ERT query also revealed that the project area intersects two special areas comprising the 
Apache/Navajo Counties Wildlife Diffuse Movement Area and a statewide important connectivity zone 
(ICZ) (AZGFD 2024b). Diffuse movement areas are defined as “a type of wildlife linkage in which 
animals move within a habitat block across a relatively broad area, rather than between habitat blocks 
through a well-defined linkage” (AZGFD 2012). The ICZs were developed as part of a statewide 
connectivity assessment that identified ICZs or general areas throughout the landscape that contribute 
most to the permeability of the whole landscape (Perkl 2013). 
The National Audubon Society directs an effort to identify, monitor, and protect critical bird habitat 
throughout the United States. These critical habitats, known as Important Bird Areas (IBAs), are essential 
in the life history of bird species. In review of the National Audubon Society IBA (National Audubon 
Society 2023), there are no IBAs in or near the project area. 
The Pacific Flyway is a bird migration corridor that extends from the Arctic tundra of Alaska and 
Canada’s western territories southward across the Intermountain West and Pacific coast of the continental 
United States to the Central and South American Pacific coastal regions (USFWS 2024e). Each year, 
migratory birds enroute to and from breeding grounds travel the Pacific Flyway that provides critical 
habitats to sustain the birds’ migration (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration 2012). 
The state of Arizona lies within the eastern expansion of the Pacific Flyway. 
The project area is not within any ungulate migration routes (U.S. Geological Survey 2022). 
Arizona Department of Agriculture Native Plant Law 
The AZNPL (Arizona Revised Statutes 3-904) (AZDA 2024a) protects certain native plants on private 
and public lands in Arizona. The only exception to this law is for plant removal on federal and tribal 
lands, in which case the federal land management agency or the tribe must be contacted directly for 
guidance on their requirements for native plants. Harvest and transport of native plants or native plant 
materials from any land, including private land, requires permission from the landowner and a permit 
from the AZDA. The AZDA also requires notification before land clearing is undertaken, even if the

<!-- page 724 -->
Biological Resources Memorandum for the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project in Navajo County, Arizona / 
SWCA Project No. 83604 
24 
plants would be destroyed or salvaged and replanted off-site. Appendix D provides the AZDA’s Notice of 
Intent to Clear Land form, which lists submittal deadlines based on the acreage of vegetation removal. 
A separate application is required for the permits necessary to salvage and transport protected native 
plants off-site. The landowner has the right to transplant on-site or to destroy any plants occurring on the 
property without permits. 
Plants protected by the AZNPL were observed in the project area including banana yucca (Yucca 
baccata), narrowleaf yucca (Yucca angustissima), tulip pricklypear (Opuntia phaeacantha), plains 
pricklypear (Opuntia polyacantha), Whipple cholla (Cylindropuntia whipplei), and grama grass cactus 
(Sclerocactus papyracanthus). Although a full native plant inventory was not completed for this report, 
see Table 1 for all plant species observed in the project area. If native plants cannot be avoided during 
construction, the AZDA Notice of Intent to Clear Land form (see Appendix D) must be completed and 
submitted to the AZDA before any land-clearing activities are undertaken. 
Arizona Department of Agriculture Noxious Weed Regulations 
Two restrictions have been developed to control noxious weeds in Arizona (the AZDA definitions of the 
three classes of noxious weeds are given below). First, a Class A, B, or C noxious weed or a commodity 
infested or contaminated with a Class A, B, or C noxious weed cannot be admitted into the state unless 
otherwise authorized by the AZDA. Second, the AZDA may quarantine and abate an area infested 
or contaminated with a Class A or Class B noxious weed if it has been determined that an imminent threat 
to agriculture or horticulture exists. 
The AZDA defines three classes of noxious weeds in the state of Arizona (Arizona Administrative Code 
R3-4-245) (AZDA 2024b): 
• Class A is categorized as a species of plant that is not known to exist or that is of limited 
distribution in the state and is a high-priority pest for quarantine, control, or mitigation. 
• Class B is categorized as a species of plant that is known to occur but that is of limited 
distribution in the state and may be a high-priority pest for quarantine, control, or mitigation if 
a significant threat to a crop, commodity, or habitat is known to exist. 
• Class C is categorized as a species of plant that is widespread but may be recommended for active 
control based on risk assessment. 
Five-stamen tamarisk (Tamarix chinensis), which is an AZDA Class C noxious weed, was observed in the 
project area during the site visit. Other listed noxious weed species that occur along SR 377 consist of 
camelthorn (Alhagi maurorum) and Russian knapweed (Acroptilon repens), which are AZDA Class B 
noxious weeds. Cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum), which is an AZDA Class C noxious weed, occurs along 
SR 77 (iMapInvasives 2024). 
Typical best management practices (such as cleaning equipment before entering the project area and again 
before leaving the project area, as well as using weed-free materials such as soil and gravel) can minimize 
the spread of noxious weed species.

gravel) can minimize the spread of invasive and noxious weed species.

<!-- page 747 -->
BURROWING OWL PROJECT CLEARANCE GUIDANCE FOR LANDOWNERS  
 
Arizona Burrowing Owl Working Group 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The western burrowing owl ( Athene cunicularia) is 
one of the most interesting birds of prey in Arizona 
(Figure 1).  Its species name, cunicularia, means 
“miner”, in reference to this owl’s unusual habit of 
spending time underground.  It is also called the 
“rattlesnake owl”, because young burrowing owls 
make a buzzing sound that sounds like a rattlesnake 
when disturbed.  Burrowing owls can be seen during 
daylight hours, and us e underground burrows for 
nesting and escape cover.  Despite the fact they are 
active during the day and are adaptable to human 
presence, the burrowing owl can go unnoticed in an 
area due to their secretive nature.  Their use of 
burrows also makes them susceptible to impacts 
from ground disturbing activities.  
Figure 1. Adult burrowing owl. Photo by Bruce Taubert. 
 
Over the past 50 years, most burrowing owl popul ations have experienced declines throughout 
their range in North America.  Because of this  decline, these owls are protected by various 
Federal, state, and local laws.  The burrowing ow l is listed by the USFWS as a National Bird of 
Conservation Concern, listed as endangered in Canada, and threatened in Mexico. It is also listed 
as endangered, threatened, or a species of concer n in 9 U.S. States.  All owls in Arizona are 
protected federally by the Migrat ory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) and Arizona state law (ARS Title 
17).  Violation of these laws, intentional or benign, may result in prosecution.  
 
Burrowing owls are found in areas of Arizona wh ere urbanization and other human activities are 
occurring.  Arizona is one of the fastest growing st ates in the U.S., leading to frequent conflicts 
between burrowing owls and development.  Owls can be affected by disturbance and habitat loss, 
even though there may be no direct impacts to the birds themselves or their burrows.  There is 
often inadequate information about the presence of burrowing owls on a project site until ground 
disturbance is imminent.  By then, it is too late to develop a solution that is helpful to the owls or 
the developer.  These guidelines are intended to  provide information and tools than can be 
applied when there is the potential for a project or action to adversely affect burrowing owls and 
the resources that support them.  Each project a nd situation is different and should be evaluated 
for the tools and approach that is most effectiv e in allowing a project to move forward while 
achieving burrowing owl conservation.  These guidelines may not pr ovide the necessary 
procedures for every project, and we encourage coordination with the agencies and entities listed 
in the Contact section of this document (Appendix A).

<!-- page 748 -->
Arizona Game and Fish Department January 2009 
Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners Page 3 
 
  
BURROWING OWLS SURVEY PROTOCOL 
 
This guidance was developed by State, Federal,  and other burrowing owl experts to help 
individuals avoid violating the laws protecting burrowing owls.  This effort will provide a 
standardized means for conducting burrowing owl surveys in areas where burrows are likely to 
be disturbed by projects that may displace them in order to minimize impacts to the owls.  
 
This protocol involves visual surveying for owls and burrows using transects to look for 
occupancy and/or signs of occupancy.  We recommended that only individuals with proper 
training and certification conduct the survey.  Th is document will be revised as necessary, and 
updates will be provided to certified surveyors, along with any guidance related to maintaining 
certification.  Updates to this document will also be made available to the public.  To facilitate 
statewide burrowing owl management, we recomme nd that all survey areas, routes, times, and 
detections be reported to Arizona Game and Fish  Department (AGFD) within 30 days of survey 
completion.  If owls or active bur rows are detected, coordination with the appropriate agencies 
prior to initiating ground-disturbi ng activity will facilitate comp liance with the applicable laws 
(see Appendix A). 
 
 
S
UITABLE HABITAT 
 
Burrowing owl nesting habitat typically consists of dry, treeless, short-grassland or prairie plains. 
In the desert environment they nest in areas of short, open scrublands such as mesquite (Prosopis 
spp.), creosote bush ( Larrea tridentate), rabbit-brush (Chrysothanmus nauseous), and four-wing 
saltbush ( Atriplex canescens ).  They tend to be tolerant of  human presence, and will nest in 
human-modified landscapes such as: abandoned lots within rapidly developing urban areas, 
airports, golf courses, agricultu ral fields, irrigation canals, stor m drains, roadsides, and parking 
lots (Figure 2).  In the western United States , burrowing owls do not dig their own burrows, and 
therefore depend on the presence of burrowing 
mammals.  Throughout Arizona, burrowing owls 
are associated with G unnison’s prairie dogs 
(Cynomys gunnisonii ), American badgers ( Taxidea 
taxus), ground squirrels ( Spermophilus spp.), rock 
squirrels (Spermophilus variegatus ), foxes ( Vulpes 
spp.), and coyotes ( Canis latrans).  Therefore, any 
open grassland, scrubland, or park-like area devoid 
of dense tree cover a nd containing burrowing 
mammals or adequate arti ficial nest burrows (e.g., 
erosion channels or storm drain pipes) can represent 
adequate nesting, wintering or migratory habitat.  
Figure 2. Natural burrow on a wash bank. Photo by Elissa Ostergaard.

<!-- page 749 -->
Arizona Game and Fish Department January 2009 
Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners Page 4 
 
  
SURVEYOR CREDENTIALS 
  
Burrowing owl surveyors should ha ve burrowing owl survey protoc ol certifica tion (training 
provided by AGFD; see Website in  Contacts below for next date and location) with appropriate 
documentation.  
 
Completed burrowing owl survey reports provide d to AGFD should include each surveyor’s 
certification.  Certification will be awarded on an individual basis based on attendance at the 
training, and will not need to be renewed unless new information or conditions dictate substantial 
change to the survey protocol. 
 
 
S
URVEY TIMING 
 
Burrowing owls are most likely to occupy br eeding burrows between March and mid-July 
(Figure 3).  While burrowing owl migration habits are not well doc umented, it is believed that 
owls in northern Arizona genera lly migrate south for the winter , whereas a larger proportion (12 
to 61%; Conway and Ellis 2004) of owls in sout hern and western Arizon a is thought to be non-
migratory (Sheffield 1997). 
 
We recommend that preliminary surveys be 
conducted at the time of property acquisition or 
before project design to  allow time to properly 
accommodate or mitigate for owls, if present (Table 
1). We recommend avoiding project initiation in 
March due to the possibility of new owls arriving 
during construction unless all suitable burrows were 
permanently closed by a properly permitted 
individual or group before pr oject-related activities.  
If owls or occupied burrow s are detected within the 
construction area at any time during project 
implementation, burrows must be avoided (see 
below for buffer requirements) until: 1) status of the 
burrows can be determined and owls removed by 
properly permitted individuals or groups, or 2) other 
conservation measures are implemented.  
  
Surveys should be conducted within first light 
(typically ½ hour before sunrise) and 3 hours after 
sunrise, and between 2 hours before sunset until 
dusk (typically ½ hour af ter sunset).  Do not 
conduct surveys during or within 24 hours after a 
heavy rain or when wind speed is greater than 32 
km/hr (20 mi/hr). 
Figure 3. Artificial burrow with signs of occupancy. Photo by Elissa Ostergaard.

<!-- page 750 -->
Arizona Game and Fish Department January 2009 
Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners Page 5 
 
  
Table 1. Schedule for burrowing owl surveys. 
Fall or Winter Initial Survey 
Results Action 
No burrows detected None. 
Unoccupied burrows found Implement conservation measures* and conduct a 
second survey 90 days prior to grading. 
Occupied burrows or owls found Implement conservation measures* and survey 30 
days prior to grading. 
Spring or Summer Initial Survey 
Results Action 
No burrows detected None. 
Unoccupied burrows found Implement conservation measures* and conduct a 
second survey 30 days prior to grading. 
Occupied burrows or owls found See below. 
*Potential conservation measures include: 1)  collapsing all unoccupied bu rrows of suitable dimensions by a permitted individual , 2) identifying 
open space areas to be protected as a buffe r around occupied and suitable owl burrows, 3)  passive exclusion of owls, or 4) tran slocation of owls 
by a permitted individual. 
 
 
F
IELD SURVEY PROTOCOL 
 
We recommend that surveys be conducted in al l portions of the project site that fit the 
description of Suitable Habitat (see above).  Surveys are conduc ted by walking straight-line 
transects 10 m (33 ft) apar t (or arranged so that all 
ground surfaces can be seen) and looking for 
evidence of owls: individuals, burrows, and sign of 
occupancy at burrow entrances (pellets, feces or 
other “ornamentation”, feathers, prey remains, 
whitewash, etc) (Figure 4).  Transects should be 
located over the entire project area, and oriented so 
the tops and sides of all topographic features are 
examined.  For example, if the project area includes 
a wash with a steep bank, one transect should be near 
the top of the bank, and anot her near the base of the 
bank in the wash.  
Figure 4. Adult burrowing owl at an artificial burrow entrance. Photo by Bruce Taubert. 
 
At the start of each transect and every 100 m (300 ft), scan the entire visible project area for owls 
using binoculars or a spotting scope.  Record the location of all burrows (n atural and artificial).  
Burrows may include holes dug by mammals, birds, or created by erosion, pipes, spaces below 
concrete or other solid structures, etc.  Each bur row (entrance height 8 + cm [3 + in]; width 8 +

<!-- page 751 -->
Arizona Game and Fish Department January 2009 
Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners Page 6 
 
  
cm [3 + in]; burrow depth > 1 m [3 ft]) should be assessed  to determine potential use by 
burrowing owls, unless owls are present.  
 
An “active” burrow has a live owl or owls, or shows sign of recent use (e.g., fresh whitewash, 
fresh pellets, feathers, or nest ornamentation – Figure 2).  A “potentially active” burrow is one 
with evidence of previous use,  but not recent (e.g., old whitewa sh, old pellets, cobwebs over 
entrance, and/or debris at burrow entrances).  An “inactive” burrow exhibits no evidence of use 
by burrowing owls but is of suitable size for occupancy.  
 
Record the number and location of  all owls seen within or near  the project area.  Clean and 
remove all owl sign at potentially  active burrows.  Visit the site again after 2-8 days and check 
all potentially active burrows for fresh sign. 
 
 
 
S
URVEY REPORTING 
 
Record the surveys locations, date s, and the details of all burrow and owl detections (even if 
outside the construction zone), ei ther on a hard copy map or as  UTMs (Universal Transverse 
Mercator map coordinates compatible with GI S and GPS systems) using the standard form 
provided.  Attach credentials of all surveyors as described above.  Send within 30 days to 
raptors@azgfd.gov
 (preferred) or by mail:

O
WL DETECTIONS, CONSERVATION AND MITIGATION 
 
Should preliminary measures fail to prevent burrowing owl occupa ncy of a project  site during 
implementation, or if active burrows are locate d in the construction z one during construction 
activities, the owls should not be disturbed as it may violate federal and state laws.  A 35-m 
(100-ft) radius buffer, excluding all heavy machinery and foot traffic, should be set up around all 
active burrow entrances during construction and until the appropriate conservation action is 
determined (B. Fox, pers. comm.).  To perman ently accommodate owls on site, we recommend 
that a buffer of 35-m (100-ft) should remain in perpetuity between the burrows and new 
construction and managed to maintain breeding ha bitat suitability (Millsap and Bear 2000).  On-
site conservation areas should be connected to adjacent burrowing owl habitat through the use of 
habitat connections.  Conservati on areas should avoid isolation or  fragmentation of burrowing 
owl habitat.  Delineating protected  areas (fencing, cones, etc.) is encouraged as long as it does 
not enclose the owls or prevent the owls’ ability to see nearby predators.

<!-- page 752 -->
Arizona Game and Fish Department January 2009 
Burrowing Owl Project Clearance Guidance for Landowners Page 7 
 
  
If after surveys are completed and reports submitted to AGFD, burrowing owls or active or 
potentially active burrows are lo cated within the proj ect boundaries, the landowner is advised to 
contact the nearest AGFD office (see Appendix A) for direction.  Further mitigation or costs may 
be avoided if occupied owl areas can be set aside for 
at least 10 years and if su itable habitat for nesting 
and foraging will remain after development is 
finished.  If it is determined that the best option is to 
disturb and then mitigate for the disturbance of the 
owls, the owner must obtain a permit from U.S. Fish 
and Wildlife Service.  Mitigation may include 
excluding owls from disturbed burrows prior to 
construction and/or providing artificial burrows on-
site or in a different location and monitoring to 
determine the success of the actions taken.

Project Type Recommendations:
During the planning stages of your project, please consider the local or regional needs of wildlife in regards to movement,
connectivity, and access to habitat needs. Loss of this permeability prevents wildlife from accessing resources, finding
mates, reduces gene flow, prevents wildlife from re-colonizing areas where local extirpations may have occurred, and
ultimately prevents wildlife from contributing to ecosystem functions, such as pollination, seed dispersal, control of prey
numbers, and resistance to invasive species. In many cases, streams and washes provide natural movement corridors
for wildlife and should be maintained in their natural state. Uplands also support a large diversity of species, and should
be contained within important wildlife movement corridors. In addition, maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem functions
can be facilitated through improving designs of structures, fences, roadways, and culverts to promote passage for a
variety of wildlife. Guidelines for many of these can be found
at: https://www.azgfd.com/wildlife-conservation/planning-for-wildlife/planning-for-wildlife-wildlife-friendly-guidelines/.
Consider impacts of outdoor lighting on wildlife and develop measures or alternatives that can be taken to increase
human safety while minimizing potential impacts to wildlife. Conduct wildlife surveys to determine species within project
area, and evaluate proposed activities based on species biology and natural history to determine if artificial lighting may
disrupt behavior patterns or habitat use. Use only the minimum amount of light needed for safety. Narrow spectrum bulbs
should be used as often as possible to lower the range of species affected by lighting. All lighting should be shielded,
canted, or cut to ensure that light reaches only areas needing illumination.

Minimize the potential introduction or spread of exotic invasive species, including aquatic and terrestrial plants, animals,
insects and pathogens. Precautions should be taken to wash and/or decontaminate all equipment utilized in the project
activities before entering and leaving the site. See the Arizona Department of Agriculture website for a list of prohibited
and restricted noxious weeds at https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/unitedstates/az.shtml and the Arizona Native Plant
Society https://aznps.com/invas for recommendations on how to control. To view a list of documented invasive species or
to report invasive species in or near your project area visit iMapInvasives - a national cloud-based application for tracking
and managing invasive species at https://imap.natureserve.org/imap/services/page/map.html. 
To build a list: zoom to your area of interest, use the identify/measure tool to draw a polygon around your area of
interest, and select “See What’s Here” for a list of reported species. To export the list, you must have an
account and be logged in. You can then use the export tool to draw a boundary and export the records in a csv
file. 
 
Minimization and mitigation of impacts to wildlife and fish species due to changes in water quality, quantity, chemistry,
temperature, and alteration to flow regimes (timing, magnitude, duration, and frequency of floods) should be evaluated.
Minimize impacts to springs, in-stream flow, and consider irrigation improvements to decrease water use. If dredging is a
project component, consider timing of the project in order to minimize impacts to spawning fish and other aquatic species
(include spawning seasons), and to reduce spread of exotic invasive species. We recommend early direct coordination
with Project Evaluation Program for projects that could impact water resources, wetlands, streams, springs, and/or
riparian habitats.
The Department recommends that wildlife surveys are conducted to determine if noise-sensitive species occur within the
project area. Avoidance or minimization measures could include conducting project activities outside of breeding
seasons.
For any powerlines built, proper design and construction of the transmission line is necessary to prevent or minimize risk
of electrocution of raptors, owls, vultures, and golden or bald eagles, which are protected under state and federal laws.
Limit project activities during the breeding season for birds, generally March through late August, depending on species
in the local area (raptors breed in early February through May). Conduct avian surveys to determine bird species that
may be utilizing the area and develop a plan to avoid disturbance during the nesting season. For underground
powerlines, trenches should be covered or back-filled as soon as possible. Incorporate escape ramps in ditches or
fencing along the perimeter to deter small mammals and herpetofauna (snakes, lizards, tortoise) from entering ditches. In
addition, indirect affects to wildlife due to construction (timing of activity, clearing of rights-of-way, associated bridges and
culverts, affects to wetlands, fences) should also be considered and mitigated.
Based on the project type entered, coordination with State Historic Preservation Office may be required
(https://azstateparks.com/).
Based on the project type entered, coordination with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Migratory Bird Treaty Act) may be
required (https://www.fws.gov/office/arizona-ecological-services).
Vegetation restoration projects (including treatments of invasive or exotic species) should have a completed site-
evaluation plan (identifying environmental conditions necessary to re-establish native vegetation), a revegetation plan
(species, density, method of establishment), a short and long-term monitoring plan, including adaptive management
guidelines to address needs for replacement vegetation.

contact Project Evaluation Program directly at PEP@azgfd.gov.

Explanation Of This Form
1. Notice of Intent to Clear Land.
The majority of the desert plants fall into one of four groups specially protected from theft, vandalism or unnecessary
destruction.  They include all of the cacti, the unique plants like Ocotillo, and trees like Ironwood, Palo V erde and Mesquite.   In
most cases the destruction of these protected plants may be avoided if the private landowner gives prior notice to the Arizona
Department of Agriculture.
2. Notice Period.
When properly completed, this form is to be sent to the Department within the time periods described below.  Landowners/
developers are encouraged to salvage protected native plants whenever possible.
3. Information to Interested Parties.
The information in this notice will be posted in the applicable state office of the Department and mailed to those parties
(salvage operators, revegetation experts) who have an interest in these plants and may approach the landowner with the
possibility of saving the plant(s) from unnecessary destruction.

Agriculture and the time prescribed below has elapsed.  The “Confirmed” stamp only verifies that the Notice has been filed.

Citizen Participation Plan 
 
This Citizen Participation Plan is being implemented in conjunction with a proposed Special Use Permit 
(“SUP”) request to facilitate the development of a new solar and storage project.  The proposed project 
is located on approximately 9,200-acres of private land and 123-acres of Arizona State Land Department 
property in unincorporated Navajo County (the “Site”).  This Citizen Participation Plan is meant to open 
the lines of communication between the residents an d property owners in the surrounding area of the 
Site, and to facilitate the meaningful inclusion of  all interested parties in the development of this SUP 
request. 
 
A.  Parties Affected by the Application 
 
Our site is uniquely positioned in that it is predo minantly surrounded by federal and state lands, wit h 
only three neighboring properties that could potentially be impacted by our proposal. The area affected 
by this SUP request can be defined as a 300’ area a round the boundary of the Site. The development 
team will notify the property owners within this ar ea, including private property owners, and state an d 
federal agencies.  
 
B.  Notification and Information Procedures  
Direct Mail Notifications:  We will send detailed project information, includi ng a comprehensive 
description of the proposal, to the nearby property  owners. This will include contact information for a 
project representative who can answer questions and  address concerns directly. A site plan will be 
attached to assist with their review of the proposal.    
C.  Response Procedures  
 
Through the notification process described above, a ll interested parties will be able to gain a full 
understanding of the SUP application and will be ab le to contact the development team to voice their 
issues and concerns. The ways in which interested parties will be able to contact the development team 
include, but are not limited to, telephone, US Mail , personal contact, and/or email. The issues and 
concerns brought to the attention of the developmen t team will be taken into consideration and further  
communication will be initiated by the development team to fully consider those comments, and 
wherever possible, integrate them into the application and proposal throughout the application process. 
 
D.  Schedule of Completion 
 
1.  On June 11, 2024, a Neighborhood Community Meeting Waiver Request will be submitted to the 
County for review and approval.  
 
2.  Following this, the Citizen Participation Plan will  be submitted, along with the pre-application 
meeting request and required material, for review b y the Navajo County Planning and Development 
Department Staff.  The development team will make a ppropriate changes according to Navajo County 
Staff’s comments.

<!-- page 774 -->
3.  Following Navajo County Staff’s approval of this Ci tizen Participation Plan, notification to all 
interested parties will be sent out and verification of this via a notarized affidavit will be provided to the 
County. 
 
E.  Status Procedure 
 
As interested parties reply to the letters and sign age, communication will be opened between those 
citizens and the development team to address all qu estions, concerns, and comments.  The results of 
those discussions and the feedback gained will be t aken into consideration with the application.  This  
will be an ongoing aspect of the Citizen Participat ion Plan from first notification all the way to pub lic 
hearing. 
 
As a part of the application process, the developme nt team will be in close communication with the 
Navajo County Planning and Development Department t o ensure that they are fully apprised of the 
progress and inclusiveness of the citizen participation process.   
 
Prior to the public hearing, a written report will be submitted detailing the results of the Citizen 
Participation Plan.  This report will include: (1) a summary of all contact with interested parties, ( 2) a 
description of the approximate number of people tha t participated in the public participation process,  
and where they are located in relation to the Site, (3) a discussion of the results of the citizen participation 
process, including major issues and concerns identi fied by interested parties and how the development 
team has and will address them, and (4) an appendix  of information, including mailings and other 
pertinent materials that were used to help describe the public participation program.

5. DESCRIPTION OF PROJECT: Stellar is proposing to construct the Red Hills Solar and Storage Project 
(project). The project would be a 1,000-megawatt (MW) utility-scale photovoltaic solar energy 
generation facility located on approximately 9,090 acres of privately owned land and 123 acres of 
Arizona State Trust Land (project area) in unincorporated Navajo County, Arizona (Figure 1). The 
project would include a battery energy storage system (BESS), a project substation, a 920-foot-long, 
500 kilovolt (kV) generation-tie (gen-tie) transmission line connecting the project substation to the 
existing Salt River Project (SRP) Sugarloaf substation (located in the project area), an operations and 
maintenance (O&M) building, and other ancillary facilities.

9. ENVIRONMENTAL CONTEXTS 
9a. Landform: The project would be on the northwestern foothills of the White Mountains of Navajo 
County, approximately 5.5 miles northwest of the town of Snowflake. The Pink Cliffs are adjacent to 
the west, and State Route (SR) 77 bounds the eastern edge of the project area. 
9b. Elevation: The elevation is approximately 5,600 to 6,003 feet above mean sea level. 
9c. Surrounding Topographic Features: The study area contains generally rolling hills, and the Second 
Knolls in the northern portion of the proposed project area. Numerous draws and washes transect the 
proposed project area.

<!-- page 779 -->
STATE HISTORIC PRESERVATION OFFICE 
SURVEY REPORT SUMMARY FORM 
June 2024 
3 
9d. Nearest Drainage: Numerous drainages and draws, which include Sevenmile Draw, Ninemile Draw, 
and Tenmile Draw, transect the proposed project area. Silver Creek is approximately 1.5 miles east of 
the proposed project area.  
9e. Local Geology: The main geological unit that encompasses the study area is the Moenkopi 
Formation, with some Permian Sedimentary Formation in the eastern and southern portions of the 
proposed project area (Arizona Geological Survey 2024).  
9f. Vegetation: The study area is within the Arizona Upland Subdivision of the Plains and Great Basin 
Grassland and Great Basin Conifer Woodland biotic communities (Brown 1994). Common vegetation 
associated with the biotic communities include juniper (Juniperus spp.) and discontinuous bunch 
grasses.  
9g. Soils/Deposition: Soils within the study area are mapped as Leanto-Bisoodi-Arntz and Rock 
outcrop–Mellenthin-Leanto-Kech-Bisoodi (Natural Resources Conservation Service 2024). The soils are 
shallow, well-drained soils that form in sandy eolian deposits on 2 to 6 percent slopes and are not 
prime farmland. These soils are more suitable for use as rangeland and/or for recreational use. 
9h. Buried Deposits: Unlikely 
9i. Justification: The study area is not within an area where buried deposits are likely without some 
indication on the ground surface. 
10. BUILT ENVIRONMENT: The built environment consists of an overhead distribution line, a railroad, a 
transmission line substation, numerous dirt stock tanks, and dirt ranch/recreational roads. In addition, 
the Dry Lake Wind project is adjacent to the study area.

13. BACKGROUND RESEARCH RESULTS 
13a. Previous Projects within Study Area: 
According to a search of the archaeological site files and records maintained at the Arizona State 
Museum (ASM) and the AZSITE online database, 13 archaeological surveys have been conducted 
between 1976 and 2015 within the study area (Table 1); Six surveys (1976-42.ASM/A-75-80.MNA, 
2007-851.ASM, 2007-852.ASM, 2009-197.ASM, 2009-744.ASM, and 2010-305.ASM) overlap 
approximately 3 percent of the study area (Figures 3a and 3b). In 1976, the Museum of Northern 
Arizona conducted a linear survey of 25.6 miles for a proposed transmission line. This survey identified 
12 sites, none of which are within the study area (Keller 1976). In 2007, EnviroSystems Management, 
Inc. (EnviroSystems), conducted a linear survey of 6.9 miles for a proposed access road to a proposed 
substation. This survey identified five archaeological sites and six isolated occurrences (IOs), none of 
which are within the study area (Raney 2007b). In addition, EnviroSystems conducted a survey for the 
proposed substation location. This survey did not identify any cultural resources (Raney 2007b). Logan 
Simpson Design, Inc., conducted a linear survey of 58.1 miles for an Arizona Public Service proposed 
vegetation management project in 2009. This survey identified seven sites and 16 IOs, one of which is 
within the proposed project area (Walker and Rowe 2012). In 2009 and 2010, HDR Engineering, Inc. 
(HDR), conducted a large linear survey of approximately 1,600 acres for a proposed renewable energy 
project. This survey identified 10 archaeological sites and 107 IOs, one site (AZ P:8:122[ASM]) is within 
the study area (Brodbeck et al. 2010). Also in 2010, HDR conducted a linear survey for a proposed 
access road. This survey identified one archaeological site and seven IOs, none of which are within the 
study area (Brodbeck and Fackler 2010).  
Approximately 10 percent of the surrounding 0.5-mile radius of the project has been surveyed for 
cultural resources. These surveys were conducted for a possible Bureau of Land Management land 
release, a pipeline, road improvements, sub-transmission lines and substation, ranch land access, and 
mineral/gas exploration.

13b. Previously Recorded Cultural Resources within Study Area : 
Forty-four archaeological sites have been documented within a 0.5-mile radius of the study area, the 
majority of which consist of prehistoric habitation sites and artifact scatters. Seven of the sites have 
been documented within the proposed project area (Table 2; see Figures 3a and 3b): AZ P:8:102(ASM) 
is the in-use historic-era Reidhead Road, which extends from Snowflake to Halfway Ranch. This site was 
determined ineligible for the National and Arizona Registers of Historic Places (N/ARHP). AZ 
P:8:122(ASM) is a prehistoric artifact scatter that was determined eligible by SHPO in 2010. AZ 
Q:13:18(ASM) is the in-use Apache Railroad, which was constructed between McNary and Holbrook in 
1918 and served the McNary Sawmill until the late 1970s. This site has been determined eligible for the 
N/ARHP. NA12714, NA12715, NA13910, and NA14194 are all prehistoric artifact scatters that have not 
been evaluated for eligibility.  
The majority of the sites within the 0.5-mile search radius consist of prehistoric habitation sites and 
artifact scatters.

SECTION 21. DISCOVERY CLAUSE 
 
 
In the event that previously unreported cultural resources are encountered during ground-disturbing 
activities, all work must immediately cease within 30 m (100 feet) until a qualified archaeologist has 
documented the discovery and evaluated its eligibility for the ARHP or NRHP in consultation with the 
lead agency, the SHPO, and Tribes, as appropriate. Work must not resume in this area without 
approval of the lead agency. 
If human remains are encountered during ground-disturbing activities, all work must immediately 
cease within 30 m (100 feet) of the discovery and the area must be secured. The ASM must be notified 
of the discovery. Pursuant to Arizona Revised Statutes §41-844 and §41-865, work must not resume in 
this area without authorization from the ASM.

1 INTRODUCTION 
Stellar Red Hills Solar LLC (Stellar, or Applicant) is requesting a Special Use Permit (SUP) from Navajo 
County to allow the construction and operation of a 1,000-megawatt (MW) utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) 
solar energy generation facility and a 1,000-MW, 4-hour (i.e., 4,000 MW-hour [MWh]) battery energy 
storage system (BESS) known as the “Red Hills Solar and Storage Project” (project). The project is 
located on approximately 9,090 acres of privately owned land and 123 acres of Arizona State Trust land 
administered by the Arizona State Land Department (ASLD) in unincorporated Navajo County, Arizona, 
3.5 miles north of Snowflake (project area).1  
The project includes a short generation inter-tie transmission (gen-tie) line from the on-site substation to 
the proposed point of interconnection at the existing Salt River Project (SRP) Sugarloaf Substation, 
located in the project area. The project also includes an operations and maintenance (O&M) building and 
other ancillary facilities.  
The project will help SRP meet its peak electrical requirements with the help of clean renewable energy 
paired with BESS that allows solar energy to be used right when it's needed and even after the sun sets. 
The project is an economically beneficial use of land that requires very little water. In addition, the project 
will bring numerous jobs to Navajo County during construction and decommissioning, while generating 
steady tax revenues to support local schools, hospitals, and other beneficiaries throughout the 35-year 
useful life of the project.  
The key components of a Navajo County SUP application and their locations in this document are listed 
in Table 1. Table 2 presents an overview of the key elements addressed in the narrative portion of this 
SUP application.

the general project location and layout, background on the Applicant, the preliminary project narrative, 
goals, setbacks, and a high-level schedule. During these discussions, Navajo County broadly outlined 
their expectations in the SUP process, including the timeline, contents of the complete SUP package, and 
various action items (Table 3).

3 PROJECT NARRATIVE 
The project is a proposed 1,000-MW utility-scale PV solar energy generation facility with a 4,000-MWh 
BESS, an on-site substation, an O&M building, and other ancillary facilities. The project area comprises 
approximately 9,090 acres of private property and 123 acres of Arizona State Trust land administered by 
the ASLD and is located 3.5 miles north of Snowflake, Arizona, in unincorporated Navajo County.  
Solar energy has proven to be successful in rural communities across Arizona, bringing new local jobs 
and generating tax revenue to support schools, hospitals, and other beneficiaries (Rose Law Group 2023). 
Further, the project uses very little water to generate substantial economic benefits. The project will create 
500 to 600 jobs during construction and up to five full-time jobs during operations. Additionally, the 
Applicant plans to exclusively contract with Arizona-based off-takers so the energy generated by the 
project will remain within Arizona. 
Upon approval of the requested SUP, the Applicant will obtain all necessary building and septic permits 
and conduct construction activities beginning in the third quarter of 2026. The project is expected to be 
developed in a single phase and is currently expected to achieve full commercial operations by the fourth 
quarter of 2028. Please note that this development schedule is conceptual and is subject to change. The 
Applicant will not conduct any project improvements or grading until the proper permits have been 
secured.

3.1.2 Total Acreage and General Dimensions of All Facilities and 
Components 
The project area contains approximately 9,090 acres of private land and 123 acres of Arizona State Trust 
land. Most of the project area would be disturbed during construction, except for those areas with 
setbacks as specified by Navajo County in the concept review meeting. The Applicant incorporated the 
following setbacks into the design:  
• 50 feet along perimeter of the site 
• 50 feet when adjacent to wetlands 
• 50 feet when adjacent to public roads 
• 100 feet from existing transmission lines 
• 500 feet from existing wind turbines 
• 10-acre pads related to privately held mineral leases with 25-foot access roads 
The preliminary conceptual project site plan shows the proposed placement of the project components 
(see Appendix B). Additional surveys and design progress will further refine the project’s site plan and 
total area of disturbance, including the permanent locations of structures and facilities. Once construction 
is complete, the areas not permanently occupied by project components (e.g., solar arrays, roads) will be 
revegetated and restored.  
3.1.3 Primary Project Components 
The project consists of the following primary components with additional ancillary uses: 
• PV solar arrays 
• A collection system  
• On-site substation 
• A gen-tie line that delivers power to the SRP Sugarloaf Substation 
• An O&M area 
• A BESS 
• Access roads 
More detailed information regarding these components is provided in the sections below. 
3.1.3.1 SOLAR ARRAY 
Solar energy will be captured by an array of panels mounted to a single-axis tracking system. The PV 
panels convert incoming sunlight to electrical energy. The chosen PV panels will be either crystalline 
silicon or thin film and will be well suited for the desert environment due to their durability and 
reliability. PV panels may be single-sided or bi-facial. The panels rotate slowly throughout the day at 
a range of +/− 60 degrees facing east to west to stay perpendicular to the incoming solar rays and 
optimize energy generation.  
The ultimate decision for the module types and racking systems will depend on market conditions, 
availability, and environmental factors, including the recycling potential of the modules once they have

<!-- page 819 -->
Draft Special Use Permit Application Red Hills Solar and Storage Project 
 6 August 2024 
reached the end of their operational usefulness. Types of modules that may be installed include 
polycrystalline or monocrystalline silicon modules or any other commercially available PV technology. 
Solar thermal technology is not being considered. Multiple types of modules and racking systems may be 
installed across the site. 
3.1.3.2 COLLECTION SYSTEM 
Power from the solar array inverters will be delivered to the on-site substation via 34.5-kV collector lines 
that would be installed entirely within the fenced solar area.  
3.1.3.3 ON-SITE SUBSTATION 
The 34.5-kV collector lines would terminate at the on-site project substation where transformers would 
increase the voltage to 500 kV for transmission across the gen-tie line. The on-site substation would be 
constructed near the fenced O&M area. The substation would be enclosed by a 7-foot-tall chain-link fence 
with an additional foot of 3-strand barbed wire atop the fence.  
3.1.3.4 GEN-TIE LINE 
An approximately 920-foot-long overhead 500-kV gen-tie line will be constructed from the on-site 
substation to the existing SRP Sugarloaf Substation. The gen-tie line would require approximately two 
steel monopole structures measuring approximately 60 feet in height. 
3.1.3.5 OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE AREA 
The O&M area contains the O&M building, up to five parking spots for personnel totaling less than 
1,000 square feet, and nine temporary laydown yards, comprising approximately 43 acres. The O&M area 
will be fenced with security fencing, which would be an approximately 7-foot-tall chain-link fence topped 
with an additional foot of 3-strand barbed wire.  
The O&M building would include an approximately 900-square-foot mobile office trailer that would 
exclusively be used as office space. Sanitary units and hand washing stations would be provided. The 
Applicant will obtain a septic permit for those facilities prior to construction. Water for personal 
consumption would come from a permitted off-site location.  
A designated fire response staging area located next to the O&M building will ensure emergency vehicles 
have easy and unobstructed access to the site. Additionally, a water storage tank adjacent to the O&M 
building will provide a reliable and readily accessible water source in the event of a fire, enhancing the 
overall fire suppression capabilities. 
3.1.3.6 BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEM 
The BESS consists of a fenced area with up to 58 individual BESS enclosures that occupies 
approximately 40 acres in total. Each enclosure will be up to 190 feet long × 110 feet wide and 10 feet tall 
and will be mounted on 1-foot-tall concrete pad foundations. Each enclosure contains a series of 
individual batteries grouped together in banks equipped with ventilation and fire suppression equipment 
suitable for battery technology.  
3.1.3.7 SITE ACCESS 
The project is accessible from Arizona State Route 277 (SR 277) via Rocking Chair Ranch Road, an 
existing 6-mile native-surface road that crosses private land owned by Aztec Land and Cattle Company,

<!-- page 820 -->
Draft Special Use Permit Application Red Hills Solar and Storage Project 
 7 August 2024 
Ltd. (Aztec) and Rocking Chair Ranch. The project is also accessible from Arizona State Route 77 (SR 
77) via an unnamed access road across land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). 
Stellar is concurrently pursuing all necessary road agreements with Aztec and the BLM during the 
preparation of this SUP. The Applicant expects to have all road use agreements in place prior to 
construction activities.  
Internal project roads would include an all-weather compacted gravel bed up to 20 feet wide (16 feet wide 
with 2-foot shoulders on both sides). This width would provide an internal turning radius sufficiently 
sized for emergency vehicle access in compliance with the local fire code. Access roads throughout the 
project area would be topped with aggregate at a thickness of 6 to 12 inches.  
3.1.3.8 WATER USAGE AND SOURCES 
During construction, water is needed for compaction and dust control during site preparation and grading 
activities. Water will also be required for revegetation post-construction. Construction water will be 
sourced either from legally permitted water resources within the project area or transported to the site as 
needed from an off-site source. During decommissioning, water will be needed for dust control and 
post-project revegetation activities. Additionally, a water storage tank will be placed next to the O&M 
building to provide easy access in case of fire during all stages of the project, including construction, 
operations, and decommissioning. The project will store two 5-gallon jugs of potable water in the O&M 
building for workers: one jug will be for regular use, and the other will serve as a backup. 
During operations, solar panels require minimal maintenance. Solar panel manufacturers currently do not 
recommend routine washing of panels; however, periodic washing may be needed to optimize their 
performance. The solar panels may be washed up to two times per year, depending on the severity of 
soiling and effects on production, requiring approximately 20 gallons per MWh per year of water. Potable 
water used by employees in the O&M facility would be brought into the site by the employees 
themselves, as needed.  
3.1.4 Project Design Features 
3.1.4.1 EROSION CONTROL AND STORMWATER DRAINAGE 
The Applicant will comply with the Navajo County Drainage Policy, which includes submitting 
a Drainage Plan and a Drainage Report to Navajo County, preparing and implementing a Stormwater 
Pollution Prevention Plan, obtaining an Arizona Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Construction 
General Permit from the ADEQ, filing a Notice of Intent for construction with the ADEQ, and sharing 
a copy of the Notice of Intent with the County prior to construction. In advance of the Drainage Plan and 
Report, the Applicant understands that it will not increase drainage flow onto adjoining properties.  
3.1.4.2 FIRE PROTECTION 
The Applicant will consult with the Snowflake-Taylor Fire Department and the Arizona State Fire 
Officials for fire safety recommendations during construction and operation. This documentation will be 
appended to the final application. The Applicant held discussions with the Navajo County Emergency 
Manager and incorporated her comments into the SSSP, which is included with this application in 
Appendix D. If required, the Applicant will also submit a fire plan or emergency action plan to Navajo 
County prior to construction. 
Following advice from the Citizen Recommendation Review, the Applicant revised the SSSP to include a 
fire response staging area and an aboveground water storage tank for fire emergencies associated with the

<!-- page 821 -->
Draft Special Use Permit Application Red Hills Solar and Storage Project 
 8 August 2024 
O&M building. Additionally, the Applicant included safety specifications for the BESS, which features 
a modern safety system with self-contained fire suppression.  
3.1.4.3 HEALTH AND SAFETY PROGRAM 
The Applicant will implement a SSSP that includes employee training and education to minimize 
potential emergencies on the project site. The SSSP is included in Appendix D. 
3.1.5 Decommissioning 
At the end of commercial operation and upon termination of the lease and other agreements involved 
(i.e., approximately 35 years), the Applicant would be responsible for removing the aboveground and 
underground solar facilities to a depth of 36 inches. This includes removal of the solar arrays, inverters, 
transformers, electrical cabling and collection system, fencing, foundations, pilings, lighting, buildings, 
and access roads. If approved by the property owner and screened from view (per applicable zoning 
regulations), project fencing, underground cables, access roads, and/or support buildings may remain in 
place. Standard decommissioning practices would be utilized, including dismantling and repurposing, 
salvaging and recycling, or disposing of the components removed from the site. Once the components are 
removed, the site would be restored by reseeding disturbed areas with a weed-free native seed mixture 
that includes forage species suitable for livestock grazing. 
3.1.6 Neighborhood Meeting 
The project is located in an area predominantly surrounded by federal and Arizona State Trust lands, with 
only three neighboring properties that could potentially be impacted. According to Navajo County’s code 
provision in Section 2907, "An applicant may make a written request and receive a written determination 
whether, due to impractical circumstances, such as a site surrounded by State or federal lands, the 
requirement for a Neighborhood Community Meeting may be waived by the Director, or their designee. 
This request must explain why the applicant’s Citizen Review Plan provides other adequate, alternative 
opportunities for citizens to express any concerns, problems, or issues they may have with the proposal in 
advance of the public hearing." Stellar will provide a written request to the County to waive the 
requirement for a Neighborhood Community Meeting. 
To ensure that all potentially affected property owners have adequate opportunities to express any 
concerns or issues, Stellar will send detailed project information, including a comprehensive description 
of the proposal, to the nearby property owners. This will include contact information for a project 
representative who can answer questions and address concerns directly. 
3.2 Project Benefits 
The project will have a positive economic impact in Navajo County and the community by generating tax 
revenue over the 35-year useful life of the project. This revenue will go toward supporting County 
operations, schools, water districts, and fire protection. Construction of the project is anticipated to 
employ up to 500 to 600 employees over an 18-month period in Navajo County, which had a 6.4% 
unemployment rate in 2022 (U.S. Census Bureau 2022). Many of these employees will live, work, shop, 
and eat in the surrounding area, increasing economic activity at local hotels, restaurants, gas stations, and 
stores in Snowflake, Holbrook, and other surrounding communities. This short-term increase in 
employees would not cause a significant increase in the need for local services or infrastructure.

<!-- page 822 -->
Draft Special Use Permit Application Red Hills Solar and Storage Project 
 9 August 2024 
During operations, the project would create up to five full-time positions with strong and competitive 
salaries and benefits.
